newsitem.title: USA: Alaska governor fears high-seas salmon interception.
newsitem.headline: Alaska governor fears high-seas salmon interception.

text.p: Following a dismal salmon run in southwest Alaska's Bristol Bay, Gov. Tony Knowles asked the U.S. State Department to investigate interception of Alaska-bound sockeye in Russian waters.

Knowles said on Tuesday he asked Mary Beth West, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for oceans, to try to determine whether fishing vessels from other countries are targeting Alaska salmon from adjacent Russian waters.
"Any increase in high seas fishing pressure on Alaska salmon is a very serious concern that will not be taken lightly," Knowles said in a news release.
"Getting the high seas fleets off Alaska's fish was an important factor contributing to the rebound in our wild salmon stocks. We cannot and will not tolerate a resumption of this activity," he said.
Knowles press secretary, Bob King, told the Alaska Public Radio Network that Bristol Bay fishermen found net marks and scars on the fish that they caught this summer.
Until this year, Alaska had been enjoying huge runs of wild salmon, allowing successive record returns and harvests.
But this summer, Bristol Bay, site of the world's largest wild sockeye salmon runs, had a return that was only half the total predicted by Alaska and University of Washington biologists.

Although the Alaska Department of Fish and Game predicted a return of 35.8 million Bristol Bay sockeyes and University of Washington scientists predicted an even larger run, the actual run totalled only 18.6 million fish as of Aug 7, according to department statistics.
